articles.title: Quantum entanglement is key to solving 250-year-old maths problem
articles.summary: Analysis of a mathematical puzzle that Leonhard Euler deemed unsolvable in the 1700s reveals that the crucial ingredient for cracking it after all is quantum entanglement
articles.content:
Analysis of a mathematical puzzle that Leonhard Euler deemed unsolvable in the 1700s reveals that the crucial ingredient for cracking it after all is quantum entanglement

Colourful Latin squares Brendan Conley, puzzlewocky.com

Quantum entanglement is key to solving a 250-year-old mathematical puzzle – and the discovery could ultimately help build quantum computers that are more resilient to errors.

In the 1700s, according to folklore, Russian Empress Catherine the Great posed a puzzle to the polymath Leonhard Euler. Could he find a way to arrange 36 military officers from six different regiments in a 6-by-6 grid so that in each row and each column, each officer belongs to a different rank and regiment? Euler concluded that no such arrangement exists, and more than a century later another mathematician, Gaston Tarry, rigorously proved this to be correct.

After another 100 years had passed, however, the “36 officers problem” got a second life. In 2022, Karol Życzkowski at Jagiellonian University in Poland and his colleagues showed that the problem could be solved after all – if it was made quantum.

Advertisement

Now, Robin Simoens at Ghent University in Belgium and Simeon Ball at the Polytechnic University of Catalonia in Spain have built further on the 2022 work, identify the ingredient that was crucial for solving the problem: quantum entanglement.

The 36 officers problem is an example of a “Latin square”, or a square grid filled with symbols that each appear once per row and column. One famous example of a Latin square is a sudoku grid.

Życzkowski and his colleagues solved their quantum Latin square by letting each officer have a quantum mixture of ranks and regiments. For example, there could be an officer for whom it would be impossible to tell with complete certainty whether he was a captain of artillery or a major of cavalry because these options would be in a quantum superposition.

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Editor’s Highlights Sign up to newsletter

But their solution also contained an additional quantum ingredient. It required all 36 officers to be connected through the inextricable link of quantum entanglement. In fact, in solving Euler’s centuries-old problem, Życzkowski and his colleagues invented a new absolutely maximally entangled (AME) quantum state. Życzkowski says that this is equivalent to entangling four six-sided dice so much that after a person rolls two dice they can predict the outcome of rolling the remaining two.

Simoens and Ball wondered how much of this quantum correlation was really necessary. “We wanted to try to find a simpler solution that doesn’t use so much of the power of entanglement,” says Simoens.

He and Ball translated the problem of filling up the 6-by-6 grid into a specific type of mathematical graph. Then they used a computer algorithm to search through all iterations of this kind of graph, looking for a special feature that corresponded to a particular quantum state of the officers – one that would solve the problem through superposition alone, without requiring all that entanglement. But they discovered that such a solution doesn’t in fact exist.

“This shows that our solution is, in a sense, as simple as possible, since the effect of quantum entanglement is indispensable,” says Życzkowski.

The discovery may have practical value for quantum computing.

Jamie Vicary at the University of Cambridge, who co-invented quantum Latin squares, says that when AMEs are made with a quantum computer’s qubits, they can act as error-correcting codes, or states that protect the qubits from making errors during computation – which is vital if quantum computers are to have practical applications.

But how to create the best error-correcting codes is an open question, says Vicary. This means that insights into what makes them work are extremely valuable. In his view, it isn’t surprising that entanglement has proved to be a key feature. “Entanglement is really the most profound driving force of new structural phenomena quantum theory can provide,” he says.

Simoens says that he and Ball are now studying solutions of the 7-by-7 Latin square problem that are not classical, but genuinely quantum.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in solving a 250-year-old mathematical problem using quantum entanglement, which has broad implications for advancing quantum computing technology, particularly in error correction. The discovery is well-explained and highlights meaningful progress with potential large-scale benefits for society through improved quantum computers.
articles.personality_title: Quantum entanglement helps solve a 250-year-old math puzzle
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In the 1700s, the famous mathematician Leonhard Euler tried to solve a puzzle called the "36 officers problem." The challenge was to arrange 36 officers from six regiments in a 6-by-6 grid so that no rank or regiment repeated in any row or column. Euler believed it was impossible, and this was later proven true for classical arrangements.

**What happened** – Recently, scientists discovered that this old puzzle can be solved if we use quantum physics ideas, especially quantum entanglement. Researchers from Belgium and Spain showed that the key to solving the puzzle is a special quantum connection between the officers. Instead of being fixed in one rank or regiment, the officers exist in quantum mixtures, linked together through entanglement.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it connects a centuries-old math problem with modern quantum technology. The special quantum states found to solve the puzzle are similar to those that can protect quantum computers from errors. Making quantum computers work better and more reliably is a big challenge, and this research adds valuable knowledge for building stronger quantum error-correcting codes.

**What's next step** – The scientists plan to study more complex puzzles, like the 7-by-7 grid, to see if quantum solutions can be found there too. This ongoing research may lead to new ways to design quantum systems and improve quantum computing even further.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Quantum entanglement has made it possible to solve a 250-year-old math puzzle and could help create more reliable quantum computers.
articles.personality_title_fr: L'intrication quantique permet de résoudre un casse-tête mathématique vieux de 250 ans
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Au 18e siècle, le célèbre mathématicien Leonhard Euler a tenté de résoudre un casse-tête appelé « le problème des 36 officiers ». Le défi était d’organiser 36 officiers de six régiments dans une grille 6 par 6 sans que le même rang ou régiment ne se répète dans une ligne ou une colonne. Euler pensait que c’était impossible, ce qui a été prouvé plus tard pour les arrangements classiques.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Récemment, des scientifiques ont découvert que ce vieux casse-tête pouvait être résolu en utilisant des idées de la physique quantique, notamment l’intrication quantique. Des chercheurs de Belgique et d’Espagne ont montré que la clé était une connexion quantique spéciale entre les officiers. Au lieu d’avoir un rang ou régiment fixe, les officiers existent dans des mélanges quantiques liés par l’intrication.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante car elle relie un problème mathématique vieux de plusieurs siècles à la technologie quantique moderne. Les états quantiques spéciaux trouvés pour résoudre le casse-tête sont similaires à ceux qui peuvent protéger les ordinateurs quantiques des erreurs. Améliorer la fiabilité des ordinateurs quantiques est un grand défi, et cette recherche apporte des connaissances précieuses pour créer de meilleurs codes de correction d’erreurs.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques prévoient d’étudier des casse-têtes plus complexes, comme la grille 7 par 7, pour voir si des solutions quantiques existent aussi. Cette recherche continue pourrait mener à de nouvelles façons de concevoir des systèmes quantiques et d’améliorer encore l’informatique quantique.

**En résumé** – L’intrication quantique a permis de résoudre un casse-tête mathématique vieux de 250 ans et pourrait aider à créer des ordinateurs quantiques plus fiables.
articles.personality_title_es: La intrincación cuántica ayuda a resolver un problema matemático de 250 años
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En el siglo XVIII, el famoso matemático Leonhard Euler intentó resolver un problema llamado "el problema de los 36 oficiales". El reto era organizar a 36 oficiales de seis regimientos en una cuadrícula de 6 por 6 sin que se repitiera ningún rango o regimiento en filas o columnas. Euler pensó que era imposible, y más tarde se probó que así era para arreglos clásicos.

**Qué pasó** – Recientemente, científicos descubrieron que este viejo problema puede resolverse usando ideas de la física cuántica, especialmente la intrincación cuántica. Investigadores de Bélgica y España mostraron que la clave es una conexión cuántica especial entre los oficiales. En lugar de tener un rango o regimiento fijo, los oficiales existen en mezclas cuánticas conectadas por intrincación.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento es importante porque conecta un problema matemático de siglos con la tecnología cuántica moderna. Los estados cuánticos especiales usados para resolver el problema son similares a los que pueden proteger a las computadoras cuánticas de errores. Mejorar la confiabilidad de las computadoras cuánticas es un gran reto, y esta investigación aporta conocimientos valiosos para crear mejores códigos de corrección de errores.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos planean estudiar problemas más complejos, como la cuadrícula de 7 por 7, para ver si también existen soluciones cuánticas. Esta investigación continua podría llevar a nuevas formas de diseñar sistemas cuánticos y mejorar aún más la computación cuántica.

**Resumen en una frase** – La intrincación cuántica ha hecho posible resolver un problema matemático de 250 años y podría ayudar a crear computadoras cuánticas más confiables.

articles.title: Can Anthropic’s invisible watermarks curb ‘AI slop’? Researchers remain sceptical
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 13 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02503-7New Claude models will watermark text and tag images as AI-generated, as Anthropic responds to EU AI regulations.
articles.content:
The AI company Anthropic says that its Claude models will label AI-generated content with a watermark.Credit: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty

Anthropic, the firm behind the artificial-intelligence model Claude, has announced that text generated by any models launched on or after 2 August will be invisibly embedded with a watermark that indicates the output was written by AI. Meanwhile, images generated by Claude will in most cases come with metadata that contains a digital signature to show that the model processed the file.

Text-based watermarks use an algorithm to tweak how an AI model selects its wording. When applied to a stretch of text, this process leaves a statistically observable trace in the output. Anthropic, based in San Francisco, California, says that its watermark won’t change the “meaning, quality, or readability of Claude’s response” and that the mark “may persist through some editing”.

The move comes in response to the EU AI Act, which was formally adopted in 2024. As of 2 August this year, providers of frontier AI models must ensure that AI-generated outputs are detectable, or be hit with fines of up to €15 million (about US$17 million) or 3% of their global annual turnover. Models released after 2 August will have to meet the requirements immediately, whereas versions already on the market have until 2 December to do so. Anthropic says that watermarks will be applied on Claude’s outputs worldwide.

The presence of the watermark reveals little about how the model was used. Detecting one “provides a signal” that content was made with Claude, says Anthropic, but is not conclusive: the model might have been used just to summarize or translate an original human idea, for example. Equally, a lack of a watermark doesn’t mean that the text was not generated by AI. Because the watermarks are based on patterns of subtle changes in a model’s word choice, passages that are very short, or that have been paraphrased or rewritten, might no longer carry a signal.

‘Humanizer’ tool can erase signs of AI-written text — alarming scientists

The impact that such watermarks will have on academic integrity remains unclear. Given that watermarks can be stripped from text easily — for example, by using another model — they are unlikely to stop motivated people from using AI to produce fake or low-quality papers, known as AI slop, says Reese Richardson, a metascientist at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois.

But if AI firms create tools that allow others to check for the watermark — as Anthropic has said it will do — and if these tools have an acceptably low rate of false positives, some illegitimate uses of AI could be detected, says computer scientist Nihar Shah, who studies the evaluation of science at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.

Watermarks could, for example, help journal editors or conference organizers to enforce strict ‘no AI’ policies in peer reviews, as the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) 2026 did in one of its two possible review streams. Organizers of the July event added a watermark to papers distributed for peer review that generated telltale text when AI was used in review reports. They caught 506 reviewers who violated the no-AI policy. “This experience suggests that while some illegitimate AI uses may be done carefully to evade detection, many others may simply copy-paste AI outputs,” says Shah, who was behind the ICML’s watermarking process.

Invisible ink
articles.reasoning: The article reports on Anthropic's implementation of invisible watermarks in AI-generated text and images to help detect AI content, a significant technological step aligned with EU regulations. This innovation has broad implications for academic integrity, content authenticity, and responsible AI use, benefiting society by enabling detection of AI misuse and supporting transparency. The article provides sufficient detail on the watermarking method, its limitations, and real-world application in peer review, demonstrating meaningful impact beyond a niche audience.
articles.personality_title: Anthropic adds invisible watermarks to AI content to help detect misuse
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – As artificial intelligence (AI) tools create more text and images, it can be hard to tell if a piece was made by a computer or a human. The European Union (EU) passed a law requiring AI companies to make their AI-generated content easy to identify.

**What happened** – The AI company Anthropic announced that starting August 2, 2026, all new versions of its AI model Claude will include invisible watermarks in their text and digital signatures in images. These marks do not change the meaning or quality but leave a subtle pattern that shows the content was created by AI. This helps people and systems recognize AI-made content.

**Impact** – This is important because it helps stop the misuse of AI, such as copying AI-generated essays or fake scientific papers. For example, a recent conference used watermarks to find reviewers who broke rules by using AI. However, experts say watermarks can be removed or hidden if someone tries hard enough. Still, having these marks makes it easier to spot careless or dishonest use of AI.

**What's next step** – Anthropic plans to provide tools that let others check for these watermarks. This means teachers, editors, or event organizers could better detect when AI is used in ways they do not allow. Over time, this could lead to clearer rules about AI use and better trust in shared information.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Anthropic’s invisible watermarks help reveal AI-generated content, supporting efforts to detect misuse and promote responsible AI use under new EU regulations.
articles.personality_title_fr: Anthropic ajoute des filigranes invisibles aux contenus IA pour mieux détecter les abus
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Avec la multiplication des textes et images créés par l’intelligence artificielle (IA), il devient difficile de savoir si un contenu a été fait par un ordinateur ou un humain. L’Union européenne (UE) a adopté une loi obligeant les entreprises d’IA à rendre leur contenu identifiable.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – La société Anthropic a annoncé qu’à partir du 2 août 2026, toutes les nouvelles versions de son modèle IA Claude incluront des filigranes invisibles dans les textes et des signatures numériques dans les images. Ces marques ne changent ni le sens ni la qualité, mais laissent un motif subtil montrant que le contenu a été créé par une IA. Cela aide à reconnaître les contenus générés par l’IA.

**Impact** – Cela est important car cela aide à lutter contre les mauvais usages de l’IA, comme copier des essais générés par IA ou des faux articles scientifiques. Par exemple, une conférence récente a utilisé ces filigranes pour repérer des évaluateurs qui ont enfreint les règles en utilisant l’IA. Cependant, les experts expliquent que les filigranes peuvent être supprimés ou cachés si quelqu’un s’y prend bien. Néanmoins, ces marques facilitent la détection des usages négligents ou malhonnêtes de l’IA.

**Prochaine étape** – Anthropic prévoit de fournir des outils permettant aux autres de vérifier ces filigranes. Cela signifie que les enseignants, éditeurs ou organisateurs pourront mieux détecter les usages non autorisés de l’IA. À terme, cela pourrait conduire à des règles plus claires sur l’utilisation de l’IA et à une meilleure confiance dans les informations partagées.

**En une phrase** – Les filigranes invisibles d’Anthropic aident à révéler le contenu généré par l’IA, soutenant la détection des abus et une utilisation responsable de l’IA selon les nouvelles règles de l’UE.
articles.personality_title_es: Anthropic añade marcas de agua invisibles a contenido de IA para detectar usos indebidos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – A medida que las herramientas de inteligencia artificial (IA) crean más textos e imágenes, se vuelve difícil saber si un contenido fue hecho por una computadora o un humano. La Unión Europea (UE) aprobó una ley que exige a las empresas de IA hacer que sus contenidos generados por IA sean fáciles de identificar.

**Qué pasó** – La empresa Anthropic anunció que a partir del 2 de agosto de 2026, todas las nuevas versiones de su modelo de IA Claude incluirán marcas de agua invisibles en los textos y firmas digitales en las imágenes. Estas marcas no cambian el significado ni la calidad, pero dejan un patrón sutil que muestra que el contenido fue creado por IA. Esto ayuda a reconocer el contenido generado por IA.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque ayuda a detener el mal uso de la IA, como copiar ensayos generados por IA o falsos artículos científicos. Por ejemplo, una conferencia reciente usó marcas de agua para encontrar revisores que rompieron las reglas usando IA. Sin embargo, los expertos dicen que las marcas de agua pueden eliminarse o ocultarse si alguien se esfuerza. Aun así, tener estas marcas facilita detectar el uso descuidado o deshonesto de la IA.

**Próximo paso** – Anthropic planea ofrecer herramientas para que otros puedan verificar estas marcas de agua. Esto significa que profesores, editores u organizadores podrán detectar mejor cuándo se usa IA de formas no permitidas. Con el tiempo, esto podría llevar a reglas más claras sobre el uso de la IA y mayor confianza en la información compartida.

**Resumen en una frase** – Las marcas de agua invisibles de Anthropic ayudan a revelar contenido generado por IA, apoyando la detección de abusos y el uso responsable de la IA según las nuevas regulaciones de la UE.
